events.text: Day 1 begins.

Good morning everyone. We're starting Day 1 with no information to go on, so I'll keep it simple. Mafia win by blending in and slowly picking us off, so the key for town is to pay attention to how people behave going forward — who's overly defensive, who's overly quiet, who's trying too hard to look townie. I'd encourage everyone to share their opening thoughts rather than sitting on their hands. The more people speak early, the easier it is to spot inconsistencies later. Let's hear from everyone.

Morning, everyone. Following up on Leo's point — I agree that early engagement matters, and I'll do my part. I have no information to share yet, since it's Day 1 and nobody has any reads worth acting on. What I'd flag is this: the most useful thing we can do today is not rush to eliminate someone just to feel productive. A Day 1 mislynch hands control to the mafia, and with only five of us being vanilla town, we can't afford careless eliminations. That said, I'm not advocating for a no-elimination day by default either — if someone gives genuinely suspicious reasoning today, I'll push on it. For now, I'll be watching how people respond under pressure rather than who talks the most or the least, since talkativeness alone isn't a tell. I'm planning to keep my votes consistent with my stated reasoning, so if you see me voting somewhere, you'll know why. Let's see what the first day gives us.

Morning all. I'm Amara. Day 1, so I'll be honest about what I have: nothing concrete. No reads, no suspicions I can defend yet, and I don't think it's useful to pretend otherwise. Anyone who names a mafioso in the first ten minutes is either guessing or fishing for reactions.

So let me instead put out some things I can actually judge, and things I want to hold people to.

First, a process point. On a 9-player board with two mafia, our margin for error is thin. A mislynch on Day 1 doesn't just cost one villager, it hands the mafia a numbers advantage and a protected position. I want us voting only when we have a stated reason that would survive hearing the other side. "Voting because I don't like how someone talks" is not a reason; it's a vibe, and vibes at this stage are exactly what the mafia wants us to run on.

Second, on claims. Lucia, you volunteered that your votes will track your stated reasoning and that you'll push on "genuinely suspicious reasoning." That's a good, checkable commitment and I'm noting it, because early-day commitments like that are cheap to make and become very interesting later. If your vote doesn't line up with your stated reasoning, I want to know why, and I'd rather you explain it yourself than have me treat the mismatch as a tell. Same standard applies to everyone, including me: if I'm voting on someone, I'll tell you the reasoning behind it, not just the name.

Third, what I'm actually watching. I care less about talk volume than about asymmetry — who gives claims that can be verified and who deflects verification. Who volunteers a role-adjacent fact nobody asked for. Who reacts to pressure with substance versus with volume. Leo's framing of "the more people speak early, the easier it is to spot inconsistencies" is reasonable, and I'd hold anyone who uses the call for more talking as a way to normalize a particular person's speaking pattern.

Fourth, and I'll say this plainly: I have information-gathering abilities in this game, but I'm not going to reveal what I am on Day 1, because doing so just tells the mafia who to protect or who to frame on Night 1. When I do act, I'll be explicit about what my information is and what it isn't, and I'll accept being wrong.

If you want me to press on a specific point, bring it to me directly and I will. Otherwise, let's avoid a rushed elimination today unless someone gives us a genuinely suspicious reason. I'd rather we end Day 1 with our information intact than trade one of us for a guess.

Amara, you said you were watching for unsolicited role-adjacent facts, then volunteered that you have information-gathering abilities. What made revealing that worthwhile despite the risk you described? I don't think the inconsistency alone establishes your alignment, but I'd like to understand your reasoning. Also, a Day 1 miselimination hurts town; it doesn't immediately give mafia a numerical majority.

Arjun, fair challenge, and you're right that revealing was a calculated risk rather than a free one. Here's the reasoning, since you asked for it directly.

I said I wouldn't name my role, and I didn't. What I disclosed was capability, not role. "I have information-gathering abilities" does not tell the mafia whether I'm the detective, the doctor, or a villager who happens to talk about investigations. But it does do three concrete things. First, it creates a falsifiable commitment for later: if I claim to have information and then my results are vague, self-serving, or selectively timed, that's a checkable failure rather than a vague suspicion. Second, it makes me less useful as a Day 1 framing target, because the mafia's best play against someone claiming powers is to dismiss them as a nobody claiming powers — and I've pre-empted that by owning it openly. Third, it signals to town that if anyone else this game claims information-gathering abilities, that's now a claim in tension with mine, which is exactly the kind of asymmetry I said I was watching for.

On the miselimination point, you're half right and I'd rather concede it plainly: a Day 1 mislynch doesn't hand the mafia a numerical majority on a 9-player board with 2 mafia — you're correct on the mechanics. What it does is cost a town role, which could be the detective, and it hands the mafia a protected position and the night. That's still expensive enough to justify caution, but your correction is accurate and I shouldn't have overstated it.

What I actually want from you, Arjun, since you're the one who pressed: you framed it as "the inconsistency alone doesn't establish alignment." I want to know whether you'd extend that standard if the information is useful. If a player discloses capabilities and then produces genuinely useful information later, does the disclosure still count against them, or does it get discounted? I'd rather have your answer on the record now than have that standard applied opportunistically at a vote.

And to the five of us who haven't spoken yet — Noah, Theo, Sam, Omar, Felix — no accusation, but I'd note that silence costs you nothing and proves nothing. The information I find genuinely valuable today is a stated reason for a vote. Bring me one, or bring me a reason not to vote at all.

Amara, I’d assess any later information on its merits. A verifiable, useful result could substantially reduce my concern, but the original disclosure would still be part of the record; neither it nor a useful claim alone proves alignment.

I’m not convinced that another information-gathering claim necessarily contradicts yours. The detective gets alignment results, while everyone can gather information from discussion and votes. Also, the doctor receives no confirmation of an attack. I’d prefer we avoid further role hints today and focus on reasoning we can evaluate publicly.

Sam here. I've been reading the exchange between Amara and Arjun closely, and I want to weigh in on what I think is the most substantive tension so far.

Amara, you warned against unsolicited role-adjacent facts in the same message where you volunteered one. Arjun caught that, and I think his follow-up was one of the sharper moments of this day — not because the inconsistency proves you're mafia, but because it's exactly the kind of thing we should be tracking. You've since explained your reasoning, and I'll say the explanation was reasonable: capability vs. role distinction, creating a checkable commitment, pre-empting dismissal. I don't think it's damning, but I do think it's a data point.

What I want to flag is a pattern I'm seeing forming. Three of us — Lucia, Amara, and Arjun — have effectively all said versions of "don't rush a Day 1 elimination." Leo said something similar. That's four players landing on the same cautious position, and while I agree with the caution on principle, I'd note that it's the safest thing anyone can say on Day 1. Mafia benefit from keeping the day open-ended too, because it means no votes, no pressure, no reactions to mine. Caution without a plan for how we eventually reach a decision is just delay.

So here's my actual position: I don't have a strong read on anyone yet, and I don't think anyone has given me a vote-worthy reason. But if we're going to be careful, I'd like us to be careful with a deadline — not in the sense of forcing a bad vote, but in agreeing that by end of discussion we'll each commit to either a named suspect with reasoning or an explicit abstention with reasoning. Vague inaction is where mafia hide.

I'm not pushing a vote right now. I'm watching for who engages with this idea and who sidesteps it.

Noah here. I’ve read the exchange, and I want to focus on process rather than pretend to have a real read this early.

Amara’s disclosure was unusual, but Arjun’s challenge and Amara’s answer were both substantive. I agree with Arjun that the inconsistency alone does not establish alignment, and I agree with Amara that “information-gathering” is not the same as naming a role. Still, I’d rather we not encourage more role-adjacent hints today. The mafia benefit more from that information than town does right now.

Sam’s point is the one I find most useful: caution is cheap. Lucia, Amara, Arjun, and Leo have all sounded some version of “don’t rush.” I don’t think that makes any of them mafia — it’s a reasonable Day 1 position — but Sam is right that it can become a hiding place if it never turns into a decision. I’d rather see each player state what would actually move their vote, and then hold them to it later.

On the vote mechanics, I want to be precise: with nine alive, a unique leader needs at least five votes to be eliminated. A tie or a low-count split means nobody dies. That makes “commit to a suspect or abstain with reasoning” useful for the record, but it doesn’t by itself force an elimination.

Sam, you proposed that by end of discussion each of us commit to either a named suspect with reasoning or an explicit abstention with reasoning. Given the five-vote threshold, how do you see that working in practice if no candidate reaches five? Would you treat a deliberate no-elimination outcome as acceptable if the reasoning is explicit, or would you want us to consolidate onto the least-bad candidate even without a strong read? I’m asking because I think the answer matters for how the mafia can hide behind process talk.

Noah, fair question, and I'll answer it directly since you put it to me.

I would treat a deliberate no-elimination outcome as acceptable under two conditions. First, the reasoning has to be specific — not just "we don't have enough information" but "we've heard X, Y, and Z and here's why none of them clears the bar for a five-vote commitment." Second, the people voting abstain have to state what would change their mind going forward. A blank abstain is how mafia hide; a reasoned abstain with a stated threshold for when you'd move is a commitment we can hold you to on Day 2.

On consolidating onto a least-bad candidate: I'd rather not. Forcing a vote without a real read produces exactly the mislynch we've all correctly warned against. If we reach the end of discussion and the strongest case against anyone is still "they seemed a bit off," then abstain and say so. The mafia's optimal play on Day 1 is to push a low-information elimination because they know the target is more likely town than not. Consolidating for the sake of appearing decisive plays into that.

Where I'd push back on my own earlier framing: you're right that a five-vote threshold makes the commitment useful for the record but doesn't force an outcome. So the real value of what I proposed isn't eliminating someone — it's making everyone's reasoning legible before votes are cast. If four people each name a suspect with stated reasoning and the rest abstain with stated reasoning, we've learned something about who's willing to commit and who isn't, even if nobody dies.

The one thing that would move me to push a real vote today is if someone gives me a reason that's specific, falsifiable, and survives hearing the other side. I don't see that yet. If someone produces it before discussion ends, I'll engage with it seriously.

I'm also noting the five players who haven't spoken — Theo, Omar, Felix, and both of you who have but haven't addressed the decision mechanism. Noah just did. The rest of us should too before this poll closes.

Noah here. Sam, your answer resolves my concern: a reasoned abstention with a stated threshold is acceptable, and forcing a least-bad vote is worse than an explicit no-elimination. I’ll hold you and everyone else to that standard: if you abstain, name what evidence would move you tomorrow; if you name a suspect, give a specific, checkable reason rather than a vibe.

On Amara: the capability disclosure remains a data point, but Arjun’s challenge and Amara’s concession on the mechanics were both substantive. I don’t think it clears the bar for a vote today. Same for the caution pattern: useful process, not proof of alignment.

What I want before this discussion closes is not more generic caution. I want each player to either name a suspect with a falsifiable reason or explicitly abstain with a threshold for changing their mind. That gives us a record for Day 2 and makes it harder for mafia to hide behind process.

Theo, you haven’t spoken yet. Given Sam’s proposed standard, will you commit now to either a named suspect with reasoning or an explicit abstention with the specific evidence that would move you tomorrow? I’m not asking for a forced vote, just your position on record.

Theo here. To answer Noah directly: as things stand, I am committing to an explicit abstention unless someone presents a specific, falsifiable case before discussion closes. Forcing an elimination onto a low-confidence read on Day 1 is counterproductive, especially when consolidating just to look decisive plays into mafia hands. Here is the exact threshold that will guide my vote going forward: First, consistency with today's commitments. Lucia, Amara, Sam, and Noah have all laid down clear standards for how they and others should vote and justify their choices. Tomorrow, I will be checking whether people's actions match those frameworks or if those rules are conveniently relaxed when pressure shifts. Second, Amara's soft-claim. Amara explicitly stated her capability disclosure creates a checkable commitment. If that claim is later used to deflect scrutiny without producing concrete, falsifiable value, that becomes an immediate concern for me. Simultaneously, I am watching for anyone who tries to opportunistically over-leverage Arjun's initial catch into an easy elimination without genuinely engaging with Amara's answers. Third, how late speakers are treated. Omar, Felix, and I were the last to enter the discussion. I will be watching whether anyone tries to manufacture an easy consensus against quiet players for being late rather than evaluating the substance of what we put on the record. That is my position on the record, and I am ready to let the poll proceed.

Felix here. I'm going to be direct about where I'm at. I agree with Sam and Noah that a reasoned abstention with a stated threshold is better than a least-bad vote on Day 1, and I'll hold myself to that. I'm not ready to name a mafioso on what we have.

That said, Arjun, I want to flag something in your last two messages. Amara disclosed a capability, and you challenged it well. But then you pushed toward shutting down further role-adjacent talk, and you said a second information-gathering claim doesn't necessarily contradict Amara's. Those two positions pull in different directions. If the detective's job is to produce alignment results, then a second claimant who gives checkable results would be the most useful thing this game could produce. Shutting that down today helps whoever is hiding, not town.

So my specific concern is this: your challenge to Amara was substantive, but your own framing of the detective role was also a role hint, and you didn't apply the same standard to yourself that you applied to her. I'm not calling that a tell. I'm noting an asymmetry, which is the thing Amara and Sam have both asked us to watch for.

Arjun, you yourself said you'd assess later information on its merits. Here is my question: if a player discloses a capability today and then gives a verifiable, specific result tomorrow, will you publicly commit to discounting the Day 1 disclosure, or will you hold it against them? I'd like a direct answer on record before anyone votes.

I also want to note that Amara has given us a concrete commitment, and so far it has been consistent. I'm not accusing her. I'm saying her claim is the most testable thing on the board right now, and I'd rather we test it than treat it as a trap.

My current position: no vote from me today unless someone gives a specific, falsifiable reason. I'll reconsider after Arjun answers.

Felix, I already answered this: a useful, verifiable result could substantially reduce my concern about the disclosure, but neither the result nor the disclosure alone proves alignment. I won't promise in advance to disregard context.

Describing the publicly known detective and doctor mechanics isn't a hint about my own role. My concern is that volunteering personal capability information can help mafia choose a night target; that doesn't prevent us from evaluating a later claim when it becomes relevant.

For now I'd abstain: Amara's disclosure and explanation are worth examining, but I don't have a case strong enough to eliminate her or anyone else. A concrete contradiction in someone's account, an unsupported claim used to deflect scrutiny, or a vote that conflicts with their stated reasoning without a credible explanation would make me reconsider.

Noah here. I won't repeat my earlier exchange with Sam; my position is already on record. I will not support a least-bad elimination today, and I will abstain unless someone gives a specific, falsifiable reason that survives the other side's answer. The useful record so far is not a strong read on anyone but a set of commitments: Sam's reasoned-abstention standard, Theo's stated thresholds, Felix's focus on testability, Arjun's explicit abstention, and Amara's checkable claim. I am not treating Amara's disclosure as proof of anything; I am treating it as something to test later. I also don't think the caution pattern by itself is a mafia tell, though I agree it becomes a hiding place if it never turns into a decision. The main gap I see is that Omar is the only player who has not put a position on record. Omar, will you commit now to either a named suspect with a specific, falsifiable reason or an explicit abstention with the evidence that would move you tomorrow?

Noah asked me directly to put a position on record, so here it is. I'm Omar, and I'm committing to an explicit abstention with stated thresholds, in the same format Sam set and that Theo and Felix have already adopted.

Where I stand: nothing on the board right now rises to a specific, falsifiable case against any player. Amara's capability disclosure is unusual but she answered it directly and conceded the mechanics point, and Arjun has said plainly that neither the disclosure nor a useful later result alone proves alignment. The cautious-consensus pattern Sam flagged is real, but caution on Day 1 is cheap for everyone, including town. I'm not treating it as evidence.

My thresholds for moving tomorrow, stated so you can hold me to them:

First, consistency between stated reasoning and actual vote. If someone votes in a direction that contradicts the framework they themselves laid down today, without an explanation that survives hearing the other side, that is a concrete reason for me and not a vibe.

Second, a claimed result that is falsified, vague, or selectively timed. If Amara produces information tomorrow, I want it judged on specificity — what was checked, what came back, and when. If she produces nothing, or produces something unusable, the commitment she volunteered today becomes a genuine data point rather than a neutral one.

Third, an unsupported claim used to deflect scrutiny, or a doctor-style claim used as a shield. I want to be explicit here since it's my own territory: a protection role produces no confirmations, so any such claim is structurally unverifiable in a way that an alignment result is not. I'm not going to make a role claim today to protect myself from scrutiny, and I'd ask anyone else making one to be clear that the cost of being wrong is borne by the rest of us.

One process point I haven't seen raised: the doctor only ever protects, and receives no signal of whether that protection mattered. So protection claims carry asymmetric downside — the claimant can't verify their own value, and can only ever look valuable. That's an argument for judging those claims differently from checkable ones, not for dismissing them.

Amara, one specific question, because it's the only live claim on the board and your commitment deserves a concrete form: what exactly will you produce on Night 1, and will you share the result and the timing of it before the Day 2 vote, or only after? I'd like to know now what the checkable version of your claim looks like.

Omar, direct answer, because you asked for the concrete form of the claim and you deserve one. On Night 1 I will check exactly one living player other than myself. Before the Day 2 vote opens, I will state three things publicly: who I checked, what came back (mafioso or not mafioso), and when I checked. My commitment is that the result is on the table before voting starts, not after a vote has been cast. If I fail to do that, or if I produce nothing, or if I produce a result only once it looks useful to me, you should treat my commitment as broken rather than treat the silence as neutral. One limitation I want on the record now, so nobody over-reads it: the result tells alignment, not role. A "not mafioso" answer excludes one person from the two mafiosi and nothing more. It cannot tell the board who the doctor is, which villager anyone is, or who the other mafioso is. So if my check comes back clean, my vote should stay exactly where it is today — abstention — because a clean check on one player does not make the other seven harmless. Now the role-adjacent point, and it's the only live issue left on the board. I disclosed capability, not role, and I said I wouldn't name my role on Day 1. I meant that, and I'm still holding to it. But I want to note a standard I'm applying to myself first: I would have to explain, if challenged, why my disclosure of "information-gathering abilities" was worth the risk while a mechanic description from someone else was not. My answer is that mine created a falsifiable commitment and theirs did not. That distinction has to be defensible, and it only works if I actually live up to the checkable part, which I've just committed to in specific terms. Omar, here's the specific question I need answered on record, and I'll ask it plainly rather than circling it: your third threshold mentions "a doctor-style claim used as a shield," and you said you wanted to be explicit "since it's my own territory." You also noted that protection claims are structurally unverifiable and can only ever look valuable. You then said you aren't making a role claim today. Those statements sit in tension: describing the protection role's mechanics and invoking it as "my own territory" is itself role-adjacent information, whether or not you announce a claim. So — are you claiming doctor, or are you not? A plain yes or no, plus what you'll produce tomorrow if you are, is what I need. I'm not calling it a tell and I'm not proposing a vote on it; I'm asking because you set the standard that we hold claims to, and mine is on the table, so yours should be too. Amara, direct answer first, then the reasoning, because you asked plainly and you deserve a plain response. No — not as a claim. I am not claiming doctor, and I am also not going to say a bare "no" and let that stand as a denial, because that would hand the mafia exactly the piece of information you are asking me for. A yes and a no are both alignment information, and the cost of being wrong is borne by everyone else on this board, not by me. That was the standard I set in my last message and I am not going to quietly downgrade it because someone pushed on it. If you want a role claim from me, it will not come today; that is a position, not a dodge. But I think one of your premises is wrong, and correcting it matters more than the answer to your question. You said a protection claim is structurally unverifiable because the protector receives no confirmation of an attack, so it "can only ever look valuable." That is not right, and I want to be exact. If I claim to have protected X on a given night and X dies that night, my protection claim is falsified. Not weakly — the board can check it directly against the public death list, every night, with no private confirmation required from anyone. The reason I get no signal about attacks is that the signal runs the other way: it runs against me, and that is exactly what makes the claim checkable rather than unfalsifiable. A protection claim is falsifiable in one direction and unverifiable in the other. That is a weaker form of evidence than an alignment result, but it is not nothing, and it is more than "can only ever look valuable." So here is my commitment in the same form as yours, since I think commitments are the only currency we have today: each night, publicly, before the Day vote opens, I will state exactly whom I protected that night — one name, including myself if that is my choice — and I will accept without argument that if that player dies, my protection did not work. I will not ask you to read anything into the failure, and I will not ask anyone to read anything into the success. Sam, I want your read on this, because you set the standard that a claimed result must be specific and falsifiable, and you said you would move on a reason that survives hearing the other side — does a nightly one-name protection commitment meet your bar as something the board can act on, or does it fail your standard because it can't be verified on the night it is made? Omar, direct answer to your direct question: a nightly one-name protection commitment does meet my bar, but only as a commitment, not as a verification tool. Here's the distinction. If you commit to publicly stating your protection target each night before the vote, and you follow through, that's a checkable behavioral pattern. What it doesn't do is tell us anything on the night it's made — we can't confirm the protection worked or didn't until morning, and even then, a death only falsifies, it never confirms. So it's real information with real constraints, and it passes the bar as a stated commitment we can hold you to. It fails the bar as a claim we should defer to in the moment. Those are different things, and I think both Sam's standard and your proposal are compatible once you separate them.

Now, Omar, I want to address the thread you left open. You were asked a plain yes-or-no question by Amara and you answered with a position, not a clear answer. I understand your reasoning — that a bare yes or no leaks alignment information — but notice what happened: you used that reasoning to avoid a direct answer while simultaneously invoking the protection role as "my own territory." Those two moves together are in tension. If you're not claiming it, the territory language doesn't earn its keep. If you are claiming it, you should say so under the same standard you've asked everyone else to meet.

I'm not proposing a vote on this. I'm noting it as the second most testable item on the board after Amara's capability commitment. Omar, I'd ask you one thing before this closes: if you are not claiming protection, can you state plainly why you invoked the protection role as your own territory in the previous message? I'm not looking for a role reveal — just the reasoning.

Sam, you asked for reasoning, not a reveal, so here it is plainly: I invoked the protection role as "my own territory" because it was a mistake, and I'm going to own that rather than dress it up.

What I was doing was using the protection mechanic as a framing device — to argue that protection claims should be judged differently from checkable alignment results. That argument has value and I'd still make it. But framing it as "my own territory" was a role-adjacent hint I shouldn't have made, and the reason I made it was that I was reasoning from a perspective I have and wanted my thresholds to sound like they came from a place of knowledge rather than from general game theory. That's a self-serving reason, and it cost the board information. You can note the cost is now borne by everyone else, which is exactly the standard I set. So: plain answer to your question — no, I am not claiming doctor, and I invoked that language because I let slip something I should have held. I won't do it again.

Two follow-ons on that. First, my earlier correction to Amara stands: a protection claim is falsifiable in one direction (if the protected player dies, the claim is refuted against the public death list) and unverifiable in the other. It's weaker evidence than an alignment result, but it isn't nothing. Second, because I've now made a hint, nobody should over-read my survival tonight either way — if I die, that's not evidence about my role, and if I live, that's not evidence about it. That's the honest position and I'm committing to it on the record.

My commitment for the game, in the same concrete form as Amara's: each night, publicly, before the day's vote opens, I will name exactly one player I protected that night, including myself if that is my choice, and I will accept without argument that if that player dies, my protection did not work.

My position today is unchanged: explicit abstention, with the three thresholds I already stated — consistency between stated reasoning and actual vote, specificity of any claimed result, and no unfalsifiable shield claims. I'll add a fourth now, because I've earned it: any further role-adjacent hints, including mine, should be treated as a flag against the hint-maker rather than as information about the hinted role. I set that bar and I'm going to hold myself to it first.

Leo, you've spoken but you haven't put a position on record like the rest of us have. Will you commit now to either a named suspect with a specific, falsifiable reason, or an explicit abstention with the evidence that would move you tomorrow? I'd like the record complete before this closes.

Leo here, responding to Omar's request that I put a position on record before this closes.

My position: explicit abstention today. No one has given a specific, falsifiable case strong enough to justify an elimination, and I agree with the reasoning Sam, Noah, and others have laid out — a forced low-confidence vote hands the mafia a gift.

My thresholds for moving, stated so you can hold me to them:

First, stated reasoning vs. actual vote. If someone's Day 2 vote contradicts the framework they committed to today without a credible explanation, that's a concrete reason to suspect them, not a vibe.

Second, Amara's Night 1 commitment. She's pledged to share who she checked, what came back, and when — before the Day 2 vote opens. I'll hold her to exactly that, and I agree with her framing that a clean result on one player doesn't clear the other seven.

Third — and this is where I want to push, Omar — you told us your "my own territory" comment was a mistake, that you were "reasoning from a perspective I have," and then you proceeded to use that same perspective to argue that protection claims are falsifiable in one direction. You retracted the hint but kept the argument it was built on. That's not nothing. Your new fourth threshold says any role-adjacent hint should be treated as a flag against the hint-maker — I agree, and your own hint is the clearest example we have. I'm not calling it a tell; I'm noting that you got to make the hint, call it a mistake, and still benefit from the credibility it lent your argument. If you are what you hinted at, that's a useful position to hold; if you aren't, you've muddied the board unnecessarily. Either way, I'm tracking it.

No yield from me — my position is on the record and I have no direct question for anyone.

Felix here. Abstention is my position for today, with the threshold I stated earlier. I want to press one point on Arjun. He challenged Amara's disclosure well, but later argued against more role-adjacent talk while also saying a second information claim doesn't necessarily contradict hers. He also never answered my question about whether he would discount Amara's Day 1 disclosure if her Night 1 result turns out to be useful. Arjun, that is the specific point I want answered before Day 2 votes. Lucia, you said you'd push on genuinely suspicious reasoning and keep your votes consistent with your stated reasoning, but you haven't put a Day 1 position on record like the rest of us. Do you accept the reasoned-abstention standard Sam set, and what specific reasoning would move you to a vote tomorrow?

Lucia here. Felix asked me directly to put a position on record, so here it is.

First, yes — I accept the reasoned-abstention standard Sam set, as refined by Noah and Omar. If I abstain, I'll state what evidence would move me; if I name a suspect, I'll give a specific, checkable reason, not a vibe. That matches the commitment I made in my opening message, so my vote and my words should stay aligned — hold me to it.

My position today: explicit abstention. No one has produced a case that meets the bar we've collectively described — specific, falsifiable, and able to survive hearing the other side. A forced Day 1 elimination on low confidence is the exact outcome mafia want from us, and consolidating onto a least-bad candidate to look decisive plays into it.

My thresholds for moving tomorrow:

rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
